title: The problem with hash % N
idea: Modulo hashing puts each key on server `hash % N`. It spreads keys evenly, but when N changes, most keys move to a different server.
points: A hash function turns a key into the same number every time.
`hash % N` maps that number to one of N servers.
Adding or removing a server changes N, so most keys map elsewhere.
Cache entries then miss until refilled; sharded data must be copied to new owners.

steps.caption: With three servers, `hash % 3` gives every key one fixed home. Each dot takes the color of its server.
Add a fourth server. The divisor is now 4. Look at how many keys change owner.
Server B fails and the divisor drops to 3. Keys remap again, including keys that were not on B.

code.title: Counting moved keys
code.caption: A key keeps its server only if both remainders match. Add the pair `[100, 101]` to the list: a bigger cluster does not help.

pitfalls: Avoid `hash % N` for a cluster whose size changes; every resize remaps most keys.
Adding a cache server can send a wave of misses to your database.
Every client must use the same hash function, or the same key lands on different servers.

quiz.why: Only keys 0, 1 and 2 have the same remainder under both divisors. The other nine move to a different server.

takeaway: With `hash % N`, changing N remaps most keys, which is why rings exist.

starters: Why not just use hash % N for a cache cluster?
